claims.claim: The work known as the Glaphyra on the Pentateuch is a massive commentary comprising thirteen separate books: seven on Genesis, three on Exodus, and one each on Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy.
Cyril wrote the Glaphyra before the Christological controversy that erupted in 428, when the Nestorian dispute began.
The commentary was intended as a theological and pastoral guide for the clergy under Cyril’s direction, serving as a model for preaching and instruction.
The Glaphyra survives in Greek manuscript tradition and has been edited and published in a modern English translation by CUA Press in two volumes (Genesis; Exodus‑Deuteronomy).
A digitised Greek edition of the Glaphyra is available online, confirming the work’s transmission in the original language.

Although Cyril is best known for his defense of orthodoxy during the Nestorian controversy, the Glaphyra was composed before that debate and reflects his broader exegetical activity rather than a direct response to the controversy.
Cyril’s commentary frequently concludes sections with practical spiritual lessons for the congregation, showing its pastoral aim beyond scholarly exegesis.
